name: Canada
sub: Toronto-style curbside Blue Bin, Green Bin and Garbage, plus hazardous-waste depots and pharmacy take-back.

banana.w: Food scraps go in the Green Bin, where they are turned into compost and biogas.

eggshell.w: Egg shells are accepted in the Green Bin with other food scraps.

coffee.w: Coffee grounds and paper filters both go in the Green Bin.

bones.w: Toronto's Green Bin takes meat, fish and poultry, bones included; they are processed industrially, not in a backyard composter.

shampoo.w: Empty plastic bottles go in the Blue Bin; put the cap back on.

polybag.w: Since 2026 Ontario's Blue Bin takes plastic bags; stuff them all into one bag. Many other provinces only take them at depots or stores.

chips.w: Ontario's 2026 Blue Bin accepts chip bags and snack wrappers; elsewhere in Canada they often still go in the garbage.

tube.w: Toothpaste tubes became Blue Bin items in Ontario in 2026; many other provinces still say garbage.

carton.w: Milk and juice cartons are recycled in the Blue Bin across Canada.

eggtray.w: Paper egg cartons go in the Blue Bin with boxboard; some cities put them in organics instead.

box.w: Flatten cardboard boxes and put them in the Blue Bin.

pizza.w: Greasy or food-soiled pizza boxes go in the Green Bin; a clean, empty box can go in the Blue Bin.

newspaper.w: Newspapers and flyers go in the Blue Bin.

jar.w: Empty glass jars go in the Blue Bin; take the lid off.

wine.w: The Blue Bin takes wine bottles, but most provinces pay a deposit refund if you return them to a store or depot.

perfume.w: Empty glass perfume bottles count as cosmetic containers in Ontario's Blue Bin; some cities say garbage.

tin.w: Rinsed food cans go in the Blue Bin.

window.w: Window glass melts differently from bottle glass, so wrap it safely and put it in the garbage.

drinkglass.w: Drinking glasses and dishes are not accepted for recycling; wrap broken pieces and put them in the garbage.

mirror.w: Mirrors are coated and cannot be recycled; wrap broken pieces and put them in the garbage.

tissue.w: Toronto takes used tissues in the Green Bin; many other cities send them to garbage.

diaper.w: Toronto's Green Bin accepts diapers; most other Canadian cities want them in the garbage.

pad.w: Toronto's Green Bin accepts pads and tampons; most other cities want them in the garbage.

battery.w: Batteries can start fires in trucks; take them to a depot or a store battery collection box.

bulb.w: CFLs contain a little mercury, so take them to a hazardous waste depot or a retailer take-back.

meds.w: Return expired medicines to any pharmacy for free, safe disposal.

paint.w: Leftover paint goes to a depot or a participating paint retailer, where it is recycled.

toy.w: Broken plastic toys are not packaging, so they go in the garbage. Toys with batteries or electronics go to e-waste.
